title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
text:
Actor extensions
Additional functionality added to Actors:
player.angle  # gets current angle in degrees
player.angle += 1  # increments angle by 1
player.scale  # gets current Actor scaling factor
player.scale = 2.0  # sets the Actor scaling factor
player.flip_v = True  # flips the Actor vertically
player.flip_v = False  # turns off vertical flip, default
player.flip_h = True  # flips the Actor horizontally
player.flip_h = False  # turns off horizontal flip, default
player.opacity = 0.6  # sets opacity, from 0.0 to 1.0
player.visible = False  # hides it; still moves and collides

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
text:
Collision rectangle
A custom collision rectangle is centered on the Actor. The first line makes it 10 wide and 20 tall; the second makes it 50 wide and 20 tall, with its center moved by (5, -5).
player.collision_rect = (10, 20)  # (width, height)
# (width, height, offset_x, offset_y)
player.collision_rect = (50, 20, 5, -5)
In draw():
player.draw_collision_rect()  # outlines it in red, for debugging

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
text:
Sprites
A Sprite is one animation: its frames, how fast to play them, and whether to loop. Give an Actor a Sprite instead of an image name, and it plays the animation by itself. Docs: Sprite Animations

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
section: Sprite from a list of images
text:
Sprite from a list of images
List image names from the images folder, in order. Only fps and loop can be given.
# a Sprite made from a list of images in the images folder
alien_walk = Sprite(["alien_beige_walk1", "alien_beige_walk2"], fps=6)
alien = Actor(alien_walk)  # a Sprite instead of an image name

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
text:
Sprite sheets

A sprite sheet is one image that holds every frame of a character’s animations, laid out in a grid. Each row is one animation (idle, walk, jump, …), and every frame is the same size. Rows and frames are counted from 0, starting at the top left.
Keep sprite sheets in the sprites folder. Each sheet there has a .md file listing its frame size and what is on each row.
Sprite Studio turns art from anywhere (sheets, GIFs, Aseprite files, folders of frames) into a sprite sheet that works here, and writes the Sprite(...) code for you.

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
text:
Sprite from a sprite sheet
# Sprites made from rows of a sprite sheet in the sprites folder
idle = Sprite("rabbit", frame_width=16, frame_height=16, row=0, frames=2, fps=3)
walk_left = Sprite("rabbit", frame_width=16, frame_height=16, row=6, frames=2, fps=8)
walk_right = Sprite("rabbit", frame_width=16, frame_height=16,row=7, frames=2, fps=8)


image_name: sprite sheet filename in the sprites folder
frame_width, frame_height: size of each frame, in pixels
row (optional): row to start from, counting from 0. Default 0.
frames (optional): number of frames. Default: the whole row.
fps (optional): frames per second. Default 10.
loop (optional): False plays once. Default True.
transparent_color (optional): color to make see-through.
spacing, margin (optional): gaps between frames and around the sheet, in pixels.

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
text:
Playing and switching Sprites: actor.sprite
Give the Actor a Sprite when you make it. Set actor.sprite to switch animations. Setting the Sprite that is already playing does nothing, so it is safe to do every frame.
rabbit = Actor(idle)  # starts by playing idle
rabbit.scale = 3  # pixel art is small, so make it bigger
if keyboard.left:
    rabbit.x -= 2
    rabbit.sprite = walk_left  # switch to another Sprite
elif keyboard.right:
    rabbit.x += 2
    rabbit.sprite = walk_right
else:
    rabbit.sprite = idle  # safe every frame: restarts only if it changed
Use actor.sprite for Sprites and actor.image for image names. Whichever you set last is what the Actor shows.

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
text:
Playing once: loop=False, animation_finished
A Sprite made with loop=False stops on its last frame. animation_finished is True once it has, so you can go back to another animation. fox.sprite == hurt checks which animation is playing.
idle = Sprite("fox", frame_width=24, frame_height=16,
              row=0, frames=5, fps=6)
hurt = Sprite("fox", frame_width=24, frame_height=16,
              row=4, frames=5, fps=8, loop=False)  # plays once
fox = Actor(idle)
if fox.sprite == hurt and fox.animation_finished:  # hurt has ended
    fox.sprite = idle  # go back to idle

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
text:
Tilesheets, tilesets, and tilemaps


Tilesheet: a .png image file that contains many small images (tiles) arranged in a grid. Each tile is a piece of the world (grass, wall, water, etc.). This is the art asset created by the artist.
Tileset: a .tsx file created in Tiled that defines how to use a tilesheet. It tells Tiled things like tile size, spacing, and any extra data. It references a tilesheet. (Tileset and tilesheet are often used interchangeably.)
Tilemap: a .tmx file created in Tiled that defines the actual level layout. It uses one or more tilesets and organizes tiles into layers (ground, walls, hazards, etc.). This is the level design.

Note: the tilesheet, tileset, and tilemap must all be stored in the maps folder of your project.
Make maps in Tiled. Docs: Tile Maps

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
text:
Tile map constants
Make your own constants and use them to compute the window size.
# our tile map constants
TILE_SIZE = 16  # length of a tile, in pixels
MAP_WIDTH = 30  # width of the tilemap, in tiles
MAP_HEIGHT = 20  # height of the tilemap, in tiles
SCALE = 2  # global scaling factor
# can use to compute screen dimensions
WIDTH = TILE_SIZE * MAP_WIDTH * SCALE
HEIGHT = TILE_SIZE * MAP_HEIGHT * SCALE

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
text:
Loading a tilemap: load_tile_map()

Use load_tile_map() to import your map made in Tiled into your game based on tile map layers.

tmx_name: path to the TMX file defining the tilemap, created in Tiled.
scale: scaling factor applied to the map for display in Pygame.

Get each layer by its name in Tiled, like level["walls"]. A layer works like a list of tiles, and every tile is an Actor, so collidelist() and for loops work on it.
Using different layers allows you to treat each kind of tile differently.
level = load_tile_map("tl1.tmx", scale=SCALE)
ground = level["ground"]  # ground / background scenery to draw
walls = level["walls"]  # obstacles for player to collide with
hazards = level["hazards"]  # "bad" objects for player collision
collectables = level["collectables"]  # "good" objects to collect

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
text:
The map, layers, and tiles

A tile map is made of three kinds of thing, each inside the one before:

The map (level) holds every layer.
A layer (walls = level["walls"]) is a list of tiles.
A tile (wall = walls[0]) is one Actor on the map.

Each method belongs to one of them. The variable before the dot tells you which: level.draw() is the map, walls.get_tile(...) is a layer, wall.set_tile_image(...) is a tile.

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
text:
Drawing a tilemap: level.draw()
Draws every layer in Tiled’s layer order, from the bottom of Tiled’s Layers list to the top: background first, foreground last. To change what’s in front, drag the layers into a new order in Tiled. Draw the player after the map so it is on top.
level.draw()  # draws every visible layer, in Tiled's layer order
rabbit.draw()  # draw the player after the map, so it is on top
Layers hidden in Tiled aren’t drawn, but still collide. Hide or show a layer in code with hazards.visible = False or True.

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
text:
Wall collisions
Example of how to handle collisions with walls. Repeat the same steps for movement in each cardinal direction, putting the edge you moved against back on the wall.
# left keyboard button pressed
if keyboard.LEFT:
    rabbit.x -= 2  # move to left
    rabbit.sprite = walk_left  # change to left sprite
    # check for collision
    collision_index = rabbit.collidelist(walls)
    # did collision occur after moving to left?
    if collision_index != -1:
        # if so, put character's left edge on right edge of wall
        rabbit.left = walls[collision_index].right

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
text:
Collecting items
collidelist() gives the index of the tile you touched in the layer. pop() that index to take it off the map.
# touching a collectable? take it off the map
item_index = rabbit.collidelist(collectables)
if item_index != -1:
    collectables.pop(item_index)
# collected them all?
if len(collectables) == 0:
    game.win()

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
text:
Hazards
# touching any hazard ends the game
if rabbit.collidelist(hazards) != -1:
    game.lose()

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
text:
Creating tiles: level.create_tile()

Columns and rows count from 0, starting at the top left. They mean two different grids:

The map is a grid of squares. col, row says which square, like (5, 2). Each layer holds at most one tile per square.
The tileset is a grid of images. tile_col, tile_row says which image, like (3, 8).

The map creates new tiles. level.create_tile(tile_col, tile_row) gives a new tile showing that image from the tileset. To find an image’s tile_col and tile_row, count across and down the tilesheet from 0.
# a new tile showing the image at col 3, row 8 of the tileset
new_wall = level.create_tile(3, 8)
If your map uses only one tileset, create_tile() uses it automatically. If it uses more than one, name the tileset to use, as it is named in Tiled: level.create_tile(3, 8, tileset="town").

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
section: Adding and removing tiles: walls.set_tile(), walls.remove_tile()
text:
Adding and removing tiles: walls.set_tile(), walls.remove_tile()
A layer adds and removes tiles by square. A new tile isn’t on the map until you add it. set_tile() replaces any tile already in that square, and remove_tile() does nothing if the square is already empty.
walls.set_tile(5, 2, new_wall)  # put it at col 5, row 2 of the map
walls.remove_tile(5, 2)  # take away the tile at col 5, row 2, if any
To remove a tile you touched, pop() the index from collidelist().

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
section: Is there a tile there? walls.get_tile() and if wall:
text:
Is there a tile there? walls.get_tile() and if wall:
get_tile(col, row) gives back the tile in a square, or None if the square is empty. None means “nothing”, and it has no methods, so using it crashes:
wall = walls.get_tile(0, 0)  # an empty square, so wall is None
wall.set_tile_image(4, 8)  # crash! None has no set_tile_image()
if wall: is True for a tile and False for None, so the code inside only runs when there is a tile:
wall = walls.get_tile(2, 5)  # a tile, or None if the square is empty
if wall:  # only if there is a tile there
    print(wall.map_col, wall.map_row)  # every tile knows its square

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
text:
Changing a tile’s image: wall.set_tile_image()
A tile can change which tileset image it shows. Find it with get_tile(), check it’s there, then change it:
wall = walls.get_tile(2, 5)  # find the tile at col 2, row 5
if wall:
    wall.set_tile_image(4, 8)  # show image col 4, row 8 instead

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
text:
Pixels and squares: level.pos_to_map(), level.map_to_pos()
The map converts between pixels and squares. level.pos_to_map(x, y) gives the col, row of the square at a position in pixels, such as a mouse click or the player. level.map_to_pos(col, row) gives the position of the center of a square.
col, row = level.pos_to_map(rabbit.x, rabbit.y)  # rabbit's square
rabbit.pos = level.map_to_pos(5, 9)  # middle of col 5, row 9
Clicking to build or knock down walls:
def on_mouse_down(pos):
    x, y = pos
    col, row = level.pos_to_map(x, y)  # the square that was clicked
    if walls.get_tile(col, row):  # is there a wall?
        walls.remove_tile(col, row)  # knock it down
    else:
        walls.set_tile(col, row, level.create_tile(3, 8))  # build one

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
section: What the map can do: level
text:
What the map can do: level
The map holds every layer.
walls = level["walls"]  # get a layer by its name in Tiled
level.draw()  # draw every visible layer
new_wall = level.create_tile(3, 8)  # create a tile from the tileset
col, row = level.pos_to_map(x, y)  # pixels -> square
x, y = level.map_to_pos(col, row)  # square -> pixels (its center)
level.x -= 3  # scroll the whole map

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
section: What a layer can do: walls
text:
What a layer can do: walls
A layer is a list of tiles.
first = walls[0]  # it's a list of tiles: [i], len(), for loops
index = rabbit.collidelist(walls)  # collisions work like any list
walls.pop(index)  # remove a tile by its index
wall = walls.get_tile(col, row)  # the tile in a square, or None
walls.set_tile(col, row, new_wall)  # put a tile in a square
walls.remove_tile(col, row)  # empty a square
walls.visible = False  # stop drawing it (it still collides)

title: Advanced Pygame Zero Cheat Sheet
section: What a tile can do: wall
text:
What a tile can do: wall
A tile is one Actor on the map.
wall.pos  # it's an Actor: pos, x, y, colliderect(), ...
wall.map_col, wall.map_row  # its square on the map
wall.tile_col, wall.tile_row  # its image in the tileset
wall.set_tile_image(4, 8)  # show another image from the tileset

title: Lists & Loops Cheat Sheet
text:
Lists


Lists: data type used to organize a collection of items.
Items in lists can be ints, strings, Actors, etc.
It is an ordered sequence of individual elements.
Accessible by index.

Note: indexes start at 0! You can also use negative indexes, which count from the end.
nums = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12]
nums[0]  # accesses 1st element - index 0
nums[2]  # accesses 3rd element - index 2
nums[-1]  # accesses last element
nums[1] = 8  # updates 2nd element
print(nums)  # prints the new list

title: Lists & Loops Cheat Sheet
text:
List operations


Definition: creating a list using square brackets [].
Access: getting a value by index.
Update: replacing a value at an index.
len(name_of_list): returns how many items are in the list.
.append(item): adds item to the end of the list.
.remove(item): removes item by value.
.pop(index): removes and returns the item at index. Removes the last item if no index is provided.
.clear(): removes all items.

pets = ["cat", "dog", "fish"]
pets[1]  # dog
pets[0] = "pig"  # ["pig", "dog", "fish"]
len(pets)  # 3
pets.remove("fish")  # ["pig", "dog"]
pets.append("rat")  # ["pig", "dog", "rat"]
item = pets.pop(0)  # ["dog", "rat"]
item = pets.pop()  # ["dog"]
pets.clear()  # []

title: Lists & Loops Cheat Sheet
text:
Looping over a list


A for loop goes through each item in a list one at a time.
The loop starts at the first item and continues to the end.
The loop iteration variable stores the current item.
The loop runs once for each item in the list.



List variable names are typically plural (enemies) and our iteration variable names are typically singular (enemy).
The iteration variable grabs a single element from the list at a time, in order.

title: Lists & Loops Cheat Sheet
text:
Drawing a list of Actors
We use a for loop to iterate/loop over a list of Actors. This shows how to draw each Actor in a list.
def draw():
    screen.clear()
    for enemy in enemies:  # one Actor at a time, in order
        enemy.draw()

title: Lists & Loops Cheat Sheet
text:
Moving a list of Actors
Another loop/list example: iterate over a list of Actors to change each individual Actor’s position by its own velocity variables.
def update():
    for enemy in enemies:  # each Actor moves by its own velocity
        enemy.x += enemy.velocity_x
        enemy.y += enemy.velocity_y

title: Lists & Loops Cheat Sheet
text:
Collisions with a list
player.collidelist(enemies) returns the index of the enemy in the list that collided with player, or -1 if there was no collision. Use != -1 just to know whether a collision happened (a lose condition). Keep the index to know which item was hit, then pop() that item from the list.
# check for enemy collision with list
if player.collidelist(enemies) != -1:  # -1 means no collision
    game.lose()  # game over

# check for collectible collision with list
collision_index = player.collidelist(gems)  # index of the gem hit
if collision_index != -1:
    # collected gem, remove from list
    gems.pop(collision_index)
    game.score += 1

title: Lists & Loops Cheat Sheet
text:
Putting it all together

Define lists as global variables at the top so they can be accessed across the program.
In this program we periodically add enemies to the screen, so start() empties the list (at start and restart) and starts a clock interval that calls spawn_enemy() every 5 seconds.
spawn_enemy() creates a new enemy Actor, sets its own pos and velocity, and appends it to the list. These apply to that one single Actor, and the variable enemy does not exist outside this function: you have to reach that Actor by iterating through enemies!
draw() loops over the list to draw each Actor; update() loops over it to move each Actor, then uses collidelist() for a lose condition and to collect gems.

# globals
enemies = []


# runs once at beginning
def start():
    enemies.clear()
    clock.schedule_interval(spawn_enemy, 5)


# create spawn callback function
def spawn_enemy():
    enemy = Actor("alien")
    enemy.pos = (100, 100)
    enemy.velocity_x = random.randint(1, 5)
    enemy.velocity_y = random.randint(1, 5)
    enemies.append(enemy)


def draw():
    screen.clear()
    for enemy in enemies:  # one Actor at a time, in order
        enemy.draw()
    for gem in gems:
        gem.draw()
    player.draw()


def update():
    for enemy in enemies:  # each Actor moves by its own velocity
        enemy.x += enemy.velocity_x
        enemy.y += enemy.velocity_y

    # check for enemy collision with list
    if player.collidelist(enemies) != -1:  # -1 means no collision
        game.lose()  # game over

    # check for collectible collision with list
    collision_index = player.collidelist(gems)  # index of the gem hit
    if collision_index != -1:
        # collected gem, remove from list
        gems.pop(collision_index)
        game.score += 1

title: Event-Driven Programming Cheat Sheet
text:
Mouse clicks: on_mouse_down()
A function that is called when a mouse button is pressed. pos is a tuple (x, y) with the coordinate where the mouse clicked; button is the mouse button that was pressed. You must store pos in a global variable to use it in update() or draw().
def on_mouse_down(pos, button):  # called when a mouse button is pressed
    global click_pos  # so update() and draw() can use the click
    if button == mouse.LEFT:  # which button was pressed
        click_pos = pos  # (x, y) where the mouse clicked

title: Event-Driven Programming Cheat Sheet
text:
Mouse buttons: mouse.<BUTTON_NAME>
Constants that represent the buttons on the mouse. Use them to compare with the button that was pressed inside on_mouse_down().
mouse.LEFT  # left button
mouse.MIDDLE  # middle button
mouse.RIGHT  # right button
mouse.WHEEL_UP  # scroll up
mouse.WHEEL_DOWN  # scroll down

title: Event-Driven Programming Cheat Sheet
text:
Key pressed: on_key_down()
Function called when a key is pressed. key represents the key that was pressed. This happens once for each time the key is pressed. Event-based!
def on_key_down(key):  # called once per key press
    if key == keys.LEFT:  # the left key was pressed
        pass  # do action when left key pressed

title: Event-Driven Programming Cheat Sheet
text:
Key released: on_key_up()
Function called when a key is released. key represents the key that was released. This happens once for each time the key is released. Event-based!
def on_key_up(key):  # called once per key release
    if key == keys.LEFT:  # the left key was released
        pass  # do action when left key released

title: Event-Driven Programming Cheat Sheet
text:
Key constants: keys.<KEY_NAME>
Constants that represent keys on the keyboard. Use them in an event listener (not update()!) to compare with key. See the rest.
keys.LEFT  # left arrow key
keys.A  # A key
keys.SPACE  # space bar
keys.ESCAPE  # Esc key

title: Event-Driven Programming Cheat Sheet
text:
Keyboard polling: keyboard.<key_name>
A Boolean expression (True/False) that tells you if the key is currently pressed. Use it in update() or in your own functions. This happens as long as the key remains pressed. Polling!
def update():
    if keyboard.left:  # True while the left key is pressed
        pass  # do something
    if keyboard.right:  # True while the right key is pressed
        pass  # do something

title: Event-Driven Programming Cheat Sheet
text:
Events vs. polling










Event-based input
Polling input




Idea
something happens → you react
you keep checking if something happened


Exp
Text notification when phone on loud. Interrupts.
Notifications silenced. You have to check your phone.


Game design
mouse input, keyboard input, timer event
checking keyboard in update()


Use case
something should happen once, as an immediate response to an action (e.g. jump button pressed)
something should continue to happen in response to an action (e.g. move while arrow pressed)



def on_key_down(key):
    if key == keys.UP:  # up key pressed
        player.y -= 10  # once per press
def update():
    if keyboard.d:  # D key held down
        player.x += 1  # every frame

title: Event-Driven Programming Cheat Sheet
text:
start()

Automatically called before the game begins: place code here to run once at the beginning.
Used to set up the initial state.
Useful later when we restart our games to reset the state and play again!

def start():  # runs once before draw()/update()
    global countdown_timer
    robot.pos = 250, 250  # reset position
    countdown_timer = 5  # reset timer

title: Event-Driven Programming Cheat Sheet
text:
Callback functions

Callback functions are functions you will define that will be called when a clock event occurs.
We pass just their name (no parentheses) to the clock.schedule() calls. Callbacks can not have arguments.
# scheduled callback for moving character to random position
def move_character():
    robot.x = random.randint(50, WIDTH - 50)
    robot.y = random.randint(50, HEIGHT - 50)
Place the clock.schedule() calls elsewhere in the code, but be careful where you put them! If you place one somewhere that gets executed every frame, you may end up scheduling a rapidly growing number of callbacks and crash your program. Placing it in start() triggers it once at the beginning:
def start():
    robot.pos = (WIDTH // 2, HEIGHT // 2)
    clock.schedule_interval(move_character, 2.0)  # every 2 seconds

title: Event-Driven Programming Cheat Sheet
text:
clock.schedule_unique(callback, delay)
Waits delay seconds, then calls callback. It cancels any previously scheduled calls to that callback function, so it only will execute once until it is scheduled again.
clock.schedule_unique(trex_jump, 0.5)  # call trex_jump in 0.5 s, just once

title: Event-Driven Programming Cheat Sheet
text:
clock.schedule(callback, delay)
Waits delay seconds, then calls callback. This adds the scheduled callback to any other calls of it already scheduled.
clock.schedule(trex_jump, 0.5)  # also call trex_jump in 0.5 s

title: Event-Driven Programming Cheat Sheet
text:
clock.schedule_interval(callback, interval)
Calls callback every interval seconds. Be careful to call schedule_interval() only once for a specific callback function. Otherwise, you will schedule additional intervals!
clock.schedule_interval(spawn_coin, 3.0)  # call spawn_coin every 3 seconds

title: Event-Driven Programming Cheat Sheet
text:
clock.unschedule(callback)
clock.unschedule(trex_jump)  # cancel all scheduled calls to trex_jump

title: Event-Driven Programming Cheat Sheet
text:
clock.clear()
clock.clear()  # unschedule everything

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
text:
Collision Rectangle (Optional)
By default an Actor collides using its whole image. Give it a smaller collision rectangle, centered on the Actor, for fairer collisions.
player.collision_rect = (10, 20)  # (width, height)
# (width, height, offset_x, offset_y)
player.collision_rect = (50, 20, 5, -5)
To see where it is, draw it in draw() after drawing the Actor:
player.draw_collision_rect()  # outlines it in red, for debugging

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
text:
What Is a Sprite?
Pygame Zero docs: Sprite Animations

A Sprite is one animation: its frames, how fast to play them, and whether to loop.
Give an Actor a Sprite instead of an image name, and it plays the animation by itself.
Two ways to make one:

a list of images from the images folder
a sprite sheet from the sprites folder

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
section: Sprite from a List of Images
text:
Sprite from a List of Images
The quickest way: list the image names in order.
# a Sprite made from a list of images in the images folder
alien_walk = Sprite(["alien_beige_walk1", "alien_beige_walk2"], fps=6)
alien = Actor(alien_walk)  # a Sprite instead of an image name

Only fps and loop can be given with a list of images.

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
text:
Sprite Sheets

A sprite sheet is one image that holds every frame of a character’s animations, laid out in a grid. Each row is one animation (idle, walk, jump, …), and every frame is the same size. Rows and frames are counted from 0, starting at the top left.
Keep sprite sheets in the sprites folder. Each sheet there has a .md file listing its frame size and what is on each row.
Sprite Studio turns art from anywhere (sheets, GIFs, Aseprite files, folders of frames) into a sprite sheet that works here, and writes the Sprite(...) code for you.

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
text:
Sprite from a Sprite Sheet
# Sprites made from rows of a sprite sheet in the sprites folder
idle = Sprite("rabbit", frame_width=16, frame_height=16, row=0, frames=2, fps=3)
walk_left = Sprite("rabbit", frame_width=16, frame_height=16, row=6, frames=2, fps=8)
walk_right = Sprite("rabbit", frame_width=16, frame_height=16,row=7, frames=2, fps=8)

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
text:
Sprite Sheet Parameters


image_name: sprite sheet filename in the sprites folder
frame_width, frame_height: size of each frame, in pixels
row (optional): row to start from, counting from 0. Default 0.
frames (optional): number of frames. Default: the whole row.
fps (optional): frames per second. Default 10.
loop (optional): False plays once. Default True.
transparent_color (optional): color to make see-through.
spacing, margin (optional): gaps between frames and around the sheet, in pixels.

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
text:
Playing a Sprite
Give the Actor a Sprite. Set actor.sprite to switch animations.
rabbit = Actor(idle)  # starts by playing idle
rabbit.scale = 3  # pixel art is small, so make it bigger
if keyboard.left:
    rabbit.x -= 2
    rabbit.sprite = walk_left  # switch to another Sprite
elif keyboard.right:
    rabbit.x += 2
    rabbit.sprite = walk_right
else:
    rabbit.sprite = idle  # safe every frame: restarts only if it changed

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
text:
Playing Once
loop=False stops on the last frame. animation_finished is True once it has.
idle = Sprite("fox", frame_width=24, frame_height=16,
              row=0, frames=5, fps=6)
hurt = Sprite("fox", frame_width=24, frame_height=16,
              row=4, frames=5, fps=8, loop=False)  # plays once
fox = Actor(idle)
if fox.sprite == hurt and fox.animation_finished:  # hurt has ended
    fox.sprite = idle  # go back to idle

fox.sprite == hurt checks which animation is playing.

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
Advanced Pygame Zero
text:
Fullscreen
Pygame Zero docs: Fullscreen


Set FULLSCREEN = True at the top of your game to start in fullscreen.
Press F11 to toggle any game between fullscreen and a window.

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
text:
Tilesheets / Tilesets / Tilemaps


Tilesheet: a .png image file that contains many small images (tiles) arranged in a grid. Each tile is a piece of the world (grass, wall, water, etc.). This is the art asset created by the artist.
Tileset: a .tsx file created in Tiled that defines how to use a tilesheet. It tells Tiled things like tile size, spacing, and any extra data. It references a tilesheet. (Tileset and tilesheet are often used interchangeably.)
Tilemap: a .tmx file created in Tiled that defines the actual level layout. It uses one or more tilesets and organizes tiles into layers (ground, walls, hazards, etc.). This is the level design.

Note: the tilesheet, tileset, and tilemap must all be stored in the maps folder of your project.

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
text:
Tile Map Constants
Make your own constants and use them to compute the window size!
# our tile map constants
TILE_SIZE = 16  # length of a tile, in pixels
MAP_WIDTH = 30  # width of the tilemap, in tiles
MAP_HEIGHT = 20  # height of the tilemap, in tiles
SCALE = 2  # global scaling factor
# can use to compute screen dimensions
WIDTH = TILE_SIZE * MAP_WIDTH * SCALE
HEIGHT = TILE_SIZE * MAP_HEIGHT * SCALE

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
text:
Loading a Tilemap

Use load_tile_map() to import your map made in Tiled into your game based on tile map layers.

tmx_name: path to the TMX file defining the tilemap, created in Tiled.
scale: scaling factor applied to the map for display in Pygame.

Get each layer by its name in Tiled, like level["walls"]. A layer works like a list of tiles, and every tile is an Actor, so collidelist() and for loops work on it.
level = load_tile_map("tl1.tmx", scale=SCALE)
ground = level["ground"]  # ground / background scenery to draw
walls = level["walls"]  # obstacles for player to collide with
hazards = level["hazards"]  # "bad" objects for player collision
collectables = level["collectables"]  # "good" objects to collect

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
text:
Map, Layers, and Tiles

A tile map is made of three kinds of thing, each inside the one before:

The map (level) holds every layer.
A layer (walls = level["walls"]) is a list of tiles.
A tile (wall = walls[0]) is one Actor on the map.

Each method belongs to one of them. The variable before the dot tells you which: level.draw() is the map, walls.get_tile(...) is a layer, wall.set_tile_image(...) is a tile.

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
text:
Drawing the Map
level.draw() draws every layer in Tiled’s layer order, from the bottom of Tiled’s Layers list to the top: background first, foreground last.
level.draw()  # draws every visible layer, in Tiled's layer order
rabbit.draw()  # draw the player after the map, so it is on top

To change what’s in front, drag the layers into a new order in Tiled.
Layers hidden in Tiled aren’t drawn, but still collide.
Hide or show a layer in code with hazards.visible = False or True.

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
text: TileMap Collisions

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
text:
Handling Wall Collisions
Repeat for each direction, putting the edge you moved against back on the wall.
# left keyboard button pressed
if keyboard.LEFT:
    rabbit.x -= 2  # move to left
    rabbit.sprite = walk_left  # change to left sprite
    # check for collision
    collision_index = rabbit.collidelist(walls)
    # did collision occur after moving to left?
    if collision_index != -1:
        # if so, put character's left edge on right edge of wall
        rabbit.left = walls[collision_index].right

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
text:
Collecting Items and Hazards
collidelist() gives the index of the tile you touched. pop() that index to take it off the map.
# touching a collectable? take it off the map
item_index = rabbit.collidelist(collectables)
if item_index != -1:
    collectables.pop(item_index)
# collected them all?
if len(collectables) == 0:
    game.win()
# touching any hazard ends the game
if rabbit.collidelist(hazards) != -1:
    game.lose()

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
text:
Creating Tiles

Columns and rows count from 0, starting at the top left. They mean two different grids:

The map is a grid of squares. col, row says which square, like (5, 2). Each layer holds at most one tile per square.
The tileset is a grid of images. tile_col, tile_row says which image, like (3, 8).

The map creates new tiles from an image in its tileset:
# a new tile showing the image at col 3, row 8 of the tileset
new_wall = level.create_tile(3, 8)

Map uses more than one tileset? Name it: level.create_tile(3, 8, tileset="town")

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
text:
Adding and Removing Tiles
A layer adds and removes tiles by square. A new tile isn’t on the map until you add it.
walls.set_tile(5, 2, new_wall)  # put it at col 5, row 2 of the map
walls.remove_tile(5, 2)  # take away the tile at col 5, row 2, if any

set_tile() replaces any tile already in that square.
remove_tile() does nothing if the square is already empty.
To remove a tile you touched, pop() the index from collidelist().

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
section: Is There a Tile There? if wall:
text:
Is There a Tile There? if wall:
get_tile() gives back the tile in a square, or None if the square is empty. None means “nothing”, and it has no methods, so using it crashes:
wall = walls.get_tile(0, 0)  # an empty square, so wall is None
wall.set_tile_image(4, 8)  # crash! None has no set_tile_image()
if wall: is True for a tile and False for None, so it only runs when there is a tile:
wall = walls.get_tile(2, 5)  # a tile, or None if the square is empty
if wall:  # only if there is a tile there
    print(wall.map_col, wall.map_row)  # every tile knows its square

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
text:
Changing a Tile’s Image
A tile can change which tileset image it shows. Find it with get_tile(), check it’s there, then change it:
wall = walls.get_tile(2, 5)  # find the tile at col 2, row 5
if wall:
    wall.set_tile_image(4, 8)  # show image col 4, row 8 instead

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
text:
Pixels and Squares
The map converts between pixel positions and squares: level.pos_to_map(x, y) turns a position in pixels into a col, row. level.map_to_pos(col, row) turns a square into the position of its center.
col, row = level.pos_to_map(rabbit.x, rabbit.y)  # rabbit's square
rabbit.pos = level.map_to_pos(5, 9)  # middle of col 5, row 9

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
section: Click to Build or Knock Down
text:
Click to Build or Knock Down
def on_mouse_down(pos):
    x, y = pos
    col, row = level.pos_to_map(x, y)  # the square that was clicked
    if walls.get_tile(col, row):  # is there a wall?
        walls.remove_tile(col, row)  # knock it down
    else:
        walls.set_tile(col, row, level.create_tile(3, 8))  # build one

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
Advanced Pygame Zero
text:
The Map: level
Holds every layer.
walls = level["walls"]  # get a layer by its name in Tiled
level.draw()  # draw every visible layer
new_wall = level.create_tile(3, 8)  # create a tile from the tileset
col, row = level.pos_to_map(x, y)  # pixels -> square
x, y = level.map_to_pos(col, row)  # square -> pixels (its center)
level.x -= 3  # scroll the whole map

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
text:
A Layer: walls
A list of tiles.
first = walls[0]  # it's a list of tiles: [i], len(), for loops
index = rabbit.collidelist(walls)  # collisions work like any list
walls.pop(index)  # remove a tile by its index
wall = walls.get_tile(col, row)  # the tile in a square, or None
walls.set_tile(col, row, new_wall)  # put a tile in a square
walls.remove_tile(col, row)  # empty a square
walls.visible = False  # stop drawing it (it still collides)

title: Advanced Pygame Zero
text:
A Tile: wall
One Actor on the map.
wall.pos  # it's an Actor: pos, x, y, colliderect(), ...
wall.map_col, wall.map_row  # its square on the map
wall.tile_col, wall.tile_row  # its image in the tileset
wall.set_tile_image(4, 8)  # show another image from the tileset

title: Lists & Loops

Creating a List


Lists: data type used to organize a collection of items.
Items in lists can be ints, strings, Actors, etc.
It is an ordered sequence of individual elements.
Accessible by index.

nums = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12]

title: Lists & Loops
text:
List Operations


Definition: creating a list using square brackets [].
Access: getting a value by index.
Update: replacing a value at an index.
len(name_of_list): returns how many items are in the list.
.append(item): adds item to the end of the list.
.remove(item): removes item by value.
.pop(index): removes and returns the item at index. Removes the last item if no index is provided.
.clear(): removes all items.

title: Lists & Loops
text:
Example
fruits = ["pear", "fig", "cherry"]
fruits[1]  # fig
fruits[0] = "grape"  # ["grape", "fig", "cherry"]
len(fruits)  # 3
fruits.remove("cherry")  # ["grape", "fig"]
fruits.append("apple")  # ["grape", "fig", "apple"]
item = fruits.pop()  # ["grape", "fig"]
item = fruits.pop(0)  # ["fig"]
fruits.clear()  # []

title: Lists & Loops
text:
Iterating Over a List


A for loop goes through each item in a list one at a time.
The loop starts at the first item and continues to the end.
The loop iteration variable stores the current item.
The loop runs once for each item in the list.

title: Lists & Loops
text:
Creating a List of Actors



Define the list as a global.
Figure out where to add new Actors. This example does it based on an interval.
Create a function to create a new Actor and append it to the list.


# globals
enemies = []


# runs once at beginning
def start():
    enemies.clear()
    clock.schedule_interval(spawn_enemy, 5)


# create spawn callback function
def spawn_enemy():
    enemy = Actor("alien")
    enemy.pos = (100, 100)
    enemy.velocity_x = random.randint(1, 5)
    enemy.velocity_y = random.randint(1, 5)
    enemies.append(enemy)

title: Lists & Loops
text:
Drawing a List of Actors

We use a for loop to iterate/loop over a list of Actors.



List variable names are typically plural (enemies) and our iteration variable names are typically singular (enemy).
The iteration variable grabs a single element from the list at a time, in order.
This shows how to draw all Actors in the list on the screen.

def draw():
    screen.clear()
    for enemy in enemies:  # one Actor at a time, in order
        enemy.draw()

title: Lists & Loops
text:
Moving a List of Actors
You can use the same style of for loop in update().
See the example below, where we update each individual Actor’s position based on its own velocity.
def update():
    for enemy in enemies:  # each Actor moves by its own velocity
        enemy.x += enemy.velocity_x
        enemy.y += enemy.velocity_y

title: Lists & Loops
section: Collisions with a List of Actors
text:
Collisions with a List of Actors

collidelist(): similar to colliderect(), but called on one Actor to detect if there’s a collision with a list of Actors.
Returns the index of the Actor in the list causing the collision (-1 if none).

# check for enemy collision with list
if player.collidelist(enemies) != -1:  # -1 means no collision
    game.lose()  # game over

# check for collectible collision with list
collision_index = player.collidelist(gems)  # index of the gem hit
if collision_index != -1:
    # collected gem, remove from list
    gems.pop(collision_index)
    game.score += 1

title: Event-Driven Programming
text:
Event-Driven Programming
Per Wikipedia, “In computer programming, event-driven programming is a programming paradigm in which the flow of the program is determined by events such as user actions (mouse clicks, key presses), timers, sensor outputs, or messages from other programs or threads.”
Events include but are not limited to:

Key presses
Mouse clicks
Mouse movements
Timers


https://pgzero-plus.readthedocs.io/en/latest/hooks.html

title: Event-Driven Programming
text:
Understanding Order
start()
while game_has_not_ended():
    process_input()
    update()
    draw()

title: Event-Driven Programming
text:
Event Listener
An event listener is a bit of code that listens/waits for an event to occur (button press, mouse click, timer expiration) and executes a series of actions when the event occurs.
Event listeners allow the game/program to change during gameplay/execution.
Can be confusing at first. Event listeners seem asynchronous from draw()/update(), but we can think about it as interrupting that flow to tell us something has happened.

title: Event-Driven Programming
text:
Mouse Events
def on_mouse_down(pos, button):
    print(f"Mouse button {button} clicked at {pos}.")


Note: There are also on_mouse_move & on_mouse_up listener functions. But not as commonly used.

pos is provided as a tuple, a list-like object that uses parentheses and cannot be changed.
pos = (x, y)
pos[0]  # x
pos[1]  # y
button = button that was clicked

title: Event-Driven Programming
text:
Mouse Buttons
def on_mouse_down(pos, button):
    if button == mouse.LEFT:
        print("Left mouse button clicked.")
    elif button == mouse.RIGHT:
        print("Right mouse button clicked.")
    else:
        print("Other mouse button clicked.")


mouse.LEFT  # left button
mouse.MIDDLE  # middle button
mouse.RIGHT  # right button
mouse.WHEEL_UP  # scroll up
mouse.WHEEL_DOWN  # scroll down

Button constants: mouse.button_name (Button Constants)

Note: There’s also on_mouse_move & on_mouse_up listener functions.

title: Event-Driven Programming
text:
Events vs. Polling










Event-based input
Polling input




Idea
something happens → you react
you keep checking if something happened


Exp
Text notification when phone on loud. Interrupts.
Notifications silenced. You have to check your phone.


Game design
mouse input, keyboard input, timer event
checking keyboard in update()


Use case
something should happen once, as an immediate response to an action (e.g. jump button pressed)
something should continue to happen in response to an action (e.g. move while arrow pressed)

title: Event-Driven Programming
section: Event-Based Keyboard Inputs: Key Event Listeners

title: Event-Driven Programming
Event-Driven Programming
section: Polling Inputs: Keyboard Polling in update()
text:
Polling Inputs: Keyboard Polling in update()


# Moves Actor as long as key is pressed
def update():
    # checks if D key is pressed
    if keyboard.d:
        player.x += 1
    # checks if A key is pressed
    if keyboard.a:
        player.x -= 1

Note: Can’t use key in update(). That info is not passed to us like in keyboard event listeners. Must use keyboard.up, keyboard.a in update().
keyboard.<key> gives us a True/False value based on whether that key is pressed. Remains True if it is pressed.
Key Constants

title: Event-Driven Programming
text:
Event-Based vs. Polling Inputs


Event-Based Inputs
Moves Actor up when key pressed. Happens once per press because on_key_down triggers once.
def on_key_down(key):
    if key == keys.UP:  # up key pressed
        player.y -= 10  # once per press
Good for single actions
Exp: jump, show other image

Polling Inputs
Moves Actor as long as key is pressed. Happens continuously because update() is called repeatedly.
def update():
    if keyboard.d:  # D key held down
        player.x += 1  # every frame
Good for continuous actions
Exp: movement, play animation

title: Event-Driven Programming
text:
Callback Functions

Callback functions are functions you will define that will be called when a clock event occurs.
In this case move_character is the callback function:
# scheduled callback for moving character to random position
def move_character():
    robot.x = random.randint(50, WIDTH - 50)
    robot.y = random.randint(50, HEIGHT - 50)
Scheduled with the clock elsewhere in code:
clock.schedule_interval(move_character, 2.0)  # every 2 seconds

title: Event-Driven Programming
text:
Make something happen later
Pygame Zero docs: Clock
We can create our time-based events using Clock methods!

clock.schedule_unique(callback, delay)

Waits for delay seconds, then calls the function callback. It cancels any previously scheduled calls to callback, so it only will execute once until it is scheduled again.
Exp: Game start delay, Game over delay before main menu.

clock.schedule(callback, delay)

Waits for delay seconds, then calls the function callback. This will add this callback to any other callback scheduled.
Exp: Spawning enemies, Triggering delayed sound.

title: Event-Driven Programming
text:
Make something happen periodically
Pygame Zero docs: Clock
Instead of scheduling something to occur after a delay, we can schedule something to occur at an interval, every X seconds. We will use this the most!

clock.schedule_interval(callback, interval)

Schedules callback to execute every interval seconds.
Exp: Periodically spawn items, Auto move NPC


Be careful where you put schedule_interval()! Often put in start() or other places where we know it will only execute once. Otherwise a new interval is added every frame, and the calls pile up fast!

title: Event-Driven Programming
text:
Make things stop happening!
Pygame Zero docs: Clock
We can cancel scheduled callbacks and scheduled intervals!

clock.unschedule(callback)

Cancels all previously scheduled callbacks for that function.
Exp: Cancel spawning and timer for game over screen.

clock.clear()

Cancels everything!
Exp: Stop spawning when moving to new level

title: Pygame Zero Basics
text:
Introduction to Pygame Zero

A library that makes it easier to create games by hiding some of the more complex Pygame syntax.
It provides functions to handle graphics, sound, and events like key/mouse input to create 2D games.
For more complex games, developers typically use game engines, like Godot, Unity and Unreal Engine.


https://pgzero-plus.readthedocs.io/en/latest/introduction.html

title: Pygame Zero Basics
text:
Pygame Zero Setup

Every Pygame Zero program starts with two import lines and ends with pgzrun.go().
# program must start with these two lines
import pgzrun
from pgzero.builtins import *

...

pgzrun.go()  # program must always end with this

title: Pygame Zero Basics
text:
The Game Loop
When the program runs, Pygame Zero calls start() once. Then draw() and update() are called over and over until the window is closed.
start() → draw() → update() → draw() → update() → …
You cannot change the names of these functions! Pygame Zero looks for these exact names.

title: Pygame Zero Basics
text:
The Game Loop
You can think of it as an infinite flipbook that is updated between frames.


https://www.mattlayman.com/blog/2019/teach-kid-code-pygame-zero/

title: Pygame Zero Basics
text:
Basic Game Structure



# program must start with these two lines
import pgzrun
from pgzero.builtins import *

# Pygame Constants
WIDTH = 500  # width of game window
HEIGHT = 500  # height of game window
TITLE = "Name of Game"  # title in game window

# define global variables
alien = Actor("alien")


# runs once at beginning before draw()/update()
def start():
    alien.pos = (200, 200)  # sets initial position


# displays the new frame
def draw():
    screen.clear()  # clears the screen
    screen.fill("darkslateblue")  # fills background color
    alien.draw()  # draws the new sprite


# updates game state between drawing of each frame
def update():
    pass  # pass means do nothing, can't have empty function


pgzrun.go()  # program must always end with this




start(): called once when the game starts, before the game loop begins. Set up the game’s starting state here.
update(): called repeatedly (about 60 times per second) to change the game’s state: move characters, check conditions, change variables.
draw(): called repeatedly to draw the current state of the game: backgrounds, shapes and characters.

title: Pygame Zero Basics
text:
Graphical User Interface (GUI)


A window with visual elements that lets the user interact with the code behind the scenes.

The origin (0, 0) is the top-left corner of the window. x increases to the right and y increases down, so the bottom-right corner is (WIDTH, HEIGHT).

WIDTH: constant that sets the screen width
HEIGHT: constant that sets the screen height

title: Pygame Zero Basics
text:
Tuples

A tuple stores several values in parentheses, separated by commas. Positions and colors are tuples. You read one value with square brackets and an index starting at 0, but you cannot change one value: you replace the whole tuple.
new_pos = (300, 400)
new_pos[0]  # 300, the x-coordinate
new_pos[1]  # 400, the y-coordinate
new_pos[0] = 100  # ERROR! Cannot modify a tuple
new_pos = (100, 400)  # correct: assign an entirely new tuple

title: Pygame Zero Basics
text:
Drawing Order




# Pygame Zero constants
WIDTH = 712
HEIGHT = 508
TITLE = "Demo Game"
def draw():
    # runs top to bottom, so draw back to front
    screen.clear()  # remove the previous frame
    screen.fill("darkslateblue")  # background first
    screen.draw.filled_circle((100, 100), 50, "red")
    screen.draw.filled_circle((125, 125), 25, "yellow")  # drawn last, so on top

title: Pygame Zero Basics
text:
Drawing Rectangles and Lines
# screen.draw.rect((x, y), (width, height), "color")
screen.draw.rect((0, 0), (100, 200), "blue")  # outlined rectangle
# screen.draw.filled_rect((x, y), (width, height), "color")
screen.draw.filled_rect((25, 50), (50, 80), "red")  # filled rectangle
# screen.draw.line((x1, y1), (x2, y2), "color")
screen.draw.line((0, 0), (100, 100), "purple")

title: Pygame Zero Basics
text:
Drawing Circles and Colors
# screen.draw.circle((x, y), radius, "color")
screen.draw.circle((250, 150), 60, "purple")  # outlined circle
# screen.draw.filled_circle((x, y), radius, "color")
screen.draw.filled_circle((120, 120), 40, "red")  # filled circle




Write a color as
Example
Meaning




a color name string
"darkturquoise"
any name from the Pygame Zero color list


an RGB tuple
(150, 0, 100)
red = 150, green = 0, blue = 100, each from 0 to 255

title: Pygame Zero Basics
text:
Drawing Text

title: Pygame Zero Basics
text:
Objects
In Pygame Zero, many things in our program are objects. An object contains:

Data: information about the object, such as its position and image
Behavior: things the object can do, such as draw()

title: Pygame Zero Basics

The Actor
An Actor is a graphic you draw in the window, like a sprite in Scratch.
robot = Actor("robot_idle")  # image: images/robot_idle.png
robot.pos = (WIDTH // 2, HEIGHT // 2)  # center of the robot
def draw():
    screen.clear()
    robot.draw()  # draw the Actor at its current position

title: Pygame Zero Basics
text:
Global Variables
In Pygame Zero, we write almost all our code in functions. How do we keep data across functions, or across many calls to update()?
Global variables!

Define them outside all functions, at the top of the file.
Any function can read them freely.
A function that changes one needs one extra step…

title: Pygame Zero Basics
text:
The global Keyword

The global keyword tells Python that a variable inside a function refers to the global variable defined outside it.







You do not need global when you are…
You do need global when you are…




only reading the variable
reassigning the variable to a new value


changing something inside it (an Actor’s position, appending to a list)
changing an int, float, bool, str or tuple



Use global variables sparingly: they make programs harder to understand and debug.

title: Pygame Zero Basics
text:
Global Variable Example
alien = Actor("alien_green")
frame = 0  # global variable: how many frames so far


def start():
    alien.pos = (0, 250)


def draw():
    screen.clear()
    alien.draw()


def update():
    global frame  # we reassign frame, so we need global
    frame += 1
    if frame % 10 == 0:  # every 10 frames
        alien.x += 1

title: Pygame Zero Basics
text:
Actor Variables
An alternative to global variables: attach your own variables to an Actor with dot notation. Only use them for values that belong to that Actor.

Built-in: x, y, pos, image…
Your own: anything you create, like velocity_x

title: Pygame Zero Basics
text:
Actor Variable Example
alien = Actor("alien_beige")


def start():
    alien.pos = (0, 500)  # pos is built in
    alien.velocity_x = 1  # velocity_x is ours
    alien.velocity_y = -1  # velocity_y is ours


def draw():
    screen.clear()
    alien.draw()


def update():
    alien.x += alien.velocity_x
    alien.y += alien.velocity_y

title: Collisions & Game State
text:
Hitbox
Per Wikipedia, “A hitbox is an invisible shape commonly used in video games for real-time collision detection. It is often a rectangle or cuboid that is attached to and follows a visible object, though circular or spheroidal shapes are also common.”
In Pygame, we have a rectangular hitbox around an Actor’s image, including any transparent space.

title: Collisions & Game State
text:
Detecting Collisions

colliderect(): method called on one Actor to detect if there’s a collision with another Actor.
Returns True if there’s a collision, False otherwise.
Also works between Actors and Rectangles.

unicorn = Actor("unicorn")
monster = Actor("monster")

if unicorn.colliderect(monster):
    game.lose()

title: Collisions & Game State
text:
Detecting Collisions with Multiple Actors
player = Actor("p1")  # create player Actor
bat = Actor("bat")  # create bat enemy Actor
coin = Actor("coin")  # create coin Actor
...
if player.colliderect(bat):  # collision with enemy
    player.health -= 1
if player.colliderect(coin):  # collision with coin
    player.money += 1

title: Collisions & Game State
text:
Collisions Are Checked Every Frame

update() runs about 60 times per second.
If two Actors stay overlapped, colliderect() is True every frame.
Collect a coin and leave it there? player.money += 1 runs 60 times a second!
Fix: move the coin (or the enemy) away right after the collision.

if player.colliderect(coin):
    player.money += 1
    coin.x = random.randint(20, WIDTH - 20)  # move it so it's only collected once

title: Collisions & Game State
text:
The game Object

game stores information about your game’s state.
Keeps everything in one place.



Instead of lots of globals:
score = 0
level = 1
timer = 0

Use:
game.score = 0
game.level = 1
game.timer = 0

title: Collisions & Game State
text:
game
game  # object that stores information about the game's state
game.state  # str: "playing", "won", "lost", "over" or "paused"
game.score  # int: starts at 0. Update it in your code.
game.level  # int: starts at 1. Update it in your code.
game.timer  # float: seconds since game started. Auto-updates.
game.frame_count  # int: frames since game started. Auto-updates.
game.timer only counts while the game is "playing".

title: Collisions & Game State
text:
What is Game State

"playing" → normal gameplay
"won" → player won
"lost" → player lost
"over" → game is over (no difference between win/lose)
"paused" → temporarily stopped

Check using:
if game.state == "playing":
    player.x += 3
Update using: game.win(), game.lose(), game.over(), etc.

title: Collisions & Game State
text:
Ending a Game
# each one also cancels everything scheduled on the clock
game.win()  # sets game.state to "won"
game.lose()  # sets game.state to "lost"
game.over()  # sets game.state to "over"

Changes game.state to "won", "lost" or "over" and clears the clock.
These only work while game.state is "playing". Once the game has ended, extra calls are ignored.

title: Collisions & Game State
text:
Pausing a Game
game.pause()  # sets game.state to "paused"
game.resume()  # sets game.state back to "playing"
While paused, game.timer and Sprite animations stop, but update() and the clock keep running.

title: Collisions & Game State
text:
Ending and Restarting
Add a number to restart the game after that many seconds:
game.win(2.5)  # like game.win(), then restart after 2.5 seconds
game.lose(3)  # like game.lose(), then restart after 3 seconds
game.over(5)  # like game.over(), then restart after 5 seconds

Everything from before still happens right away: changes game.state and clears the clock.
After that many seconds, the game restarts:

game is reset: score 0, level 1, timer 0, state "playing".
Your start() function runs again.


Note: because these are skipped unless game.state is "playing", it’s safe to call them in update() every frame. Only the first call schedules a restart.

title: Collisions & Game State
text:
Restarting Right Now
game.restart()  # starts a new game right away, from any state

Use it when the player presses a key to play again.
Does the same reset as above: resets game, then runs start() again.

The rule: win(), lose() or over() to end the game. restart() to start a new one.

title: Collisions & Game State
text:
What Goes in start()?

start() runs when the game begins and again on every restart.
Restarting only resets the values inside game. Everything else is up to start().
Put everything a fresh game needs in start(): Actor positions and your own variables.

def start():
    player.pos = (200, 200)
    enemy.pos = (400, 400)
    player.lives = 3  # set here, not at the top of the file!

title: Collisions & Game State
text:
Heads-Up Display (HUD)

Shows the player info about the current game state.
Common HUD elements: score, health, lives, time, items, etc.
HUD elements are drawn on top of the game, at the end of draw().


def draw():
    screen.clear()
    # ... draw the actors and scene here, then the HUD on top
    screen.draw.text(f"Score: {game.score}", midleft=(20, 20))
    screen.draw.text(f"Time: {int(game.timer)}", center=(WIDTH // 2, 20))
    screen.draw.text(f"Level: {game.level}", midright=(WIDTH - 20, 20))
    if game.state == "lost":
        screen.draw.text("Game over!", center=(WIDTH // 2, HEIGHT // 2))
    if game.state == "won":
        screen.draw.text("You won!", center=(WIDTH // 2, HEIGHT // 2))

title: Collisions & Game State
text:
Example
Check state in draw().
def start():  # runs at the beginning and again on every restart
    player.pos = (200, 200)
    enemy.pos = (400, 400)
    key.pos = (450, 200)  # reach the key to win
def draw():
    screen.clear()
    key.draw()
    if game.state != "lost":  # draw player if "playing" or "won"
        player.draw()
    if game.state != "won":  # draw enemy if "playing" or "lost"
        enemy.draw()
    if game.state == "won":
        screen.draw.text("You won!", midtop=(250, 20))
    if game.state == "lost":
        screen.draw.text("Game over", midtop=(250, 20))

Example: game state in a game
start() runs automatically when the game begins and again every time it restarts. draw() uses game.state to decide what to draw. update() returns right away unless the game is "playing", then calls game.lose() or game.win() when the player hits the enemy or the key.
def start():  # runs at the beginning and again on every restart
    player.pos = (200, 200)
    enemy.pos = (400, 400)
    key.pos = (450, 200)  # reach the key to win


def draw():
    screen.clear()
    key.draw()
    if game.state != "lost":  # draw player if "playing" or "won"
        player.draw()
    if game.state != "won":  # draw enemy if "playing" or "lost"
        enemy.draw()
    if game.state == "won":
        screen.draw.text("You won!", midtop=(250, 20))
    if game.state == "lost":
        screen.draw.text("Game over", midtop=(250, 20))


def update():
    if game.state != "playing":  # not playing: skip the rest
        return
    player.x += 1
    if player.colliderect(enemy):
        game.lose(5)  # "lost", then restart after 5 seconds
    if player.colliderect(key):
        game.win(3)  # "won", then restart after 3 seconds

title: Sounds & Music Cheat Sheet
text:
Tone
Generates sounds using a built-in synthesizer. tone.play(pitch, duration) plays a tone at a certain pitch for a specified length in seconds. volume goes from 0 (silent) to 1 (max), default 0.8. waveform can be "sin" (default), "square", "saw" or "triangle".
tone.play("E4", 0.5)  # plays an E in octave 4 for 0.5 seconds
tone.play("A#5", 0.25)  # plays an A sharp in octave 5 for 0.25 seconds
tone.play("Bb3", 0.75)  # plays a B flat in octave 3 for 0.75 seconds
tone.play("C4", 1, volume=0.5)  # plays C4 for 1 second at half volume
tone.play("C4", 1, waveform="square")  # plays C4 for 1 second, square wave
